Estimated Marginal Means, Contrasts, and Simple Slopes

Source: vignettes/articles/marginal-means.qmd 
library(apa7)
library(modelbased)
library(dplyr)

After an ANOVA or a regression with an interaction, readers usually want to know more than whether an effect is significant. Which groups differ? How large is the effect of a predictor at different values of a moderator? The modelbased package answers these questions, and three apa7 functions put its answers in APA-style tables:

Function Table modelbased function
apa_means Estimated marginal means with confidence intervals estimate_means
apa_contrasts Differences between means (e.g., pairwise comparisons) estimate_contrasts
apa_slopes Simple slopes of a predictor at values of a moderator estimate_slopes

Each function takes either a model or the output of the modelbased function. With a model, the other arguments (e.g., by, contrast, trend, and p_adjust) go to the modelbased function, so these two calls make the same table:

apa_contrasts(fit, contrast = "dose", p_adjust = "holm")

estimate_contrasts(fit, contrast = "dose", p_adjust = "holm") |>
  apa_contrasts()

With a model, variable names in by, contrast, and trend can be quoted or unquoted, so apa_contrasts(fit, contrast = dose) works, too, as does by = c(supplement, dose). Values, such as "hp=[sd]", can be specified in a list (e.g., list(hp = "[sd]").

Estimated Marginal Means

The ToothGrowth data set has the tooth length of 60 guinea pigs given one of three doses of vitamin C (0.5, 1, or 2 mg/day) by one of two delivery methods (orange juice or ascorbic acid). Here is a two-way ANOVA:

d_tooth <- ToothGrowth |> 
  rename(length = len,
         supplement = supp) |> 
  mutate(dose = factor(dose),
         supplement = factor(supplement, labels = c("Orange juice", "Ascorbic acid")))

fit <- lm(length ~ supplement * dose, data = d_tooth)

apa_anova(fit) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

The p_adjust argument of estimate_contrasts offers several methods, including "tukey", "bonferroni", "holm", and "fdr". The note names the method, or says that the p-values are not adjusted.

Effect sizes

The contrast tables above include Cohen’s d with its confidence interval: each difference divided by the model’s residual standard deviation (here, 3.63), as in emmeans::eff_size. The interval accounts for the uncertainty in the residual standard deviation, and the note says how d was computed. Use effect_size = FALSE to leave d out.

d is added automatically for models of continuous outcomes with an identity link, such as lm and aov. For mixed models, differences can be standardized by different standard deviations (e.g., the residual SD for differences within clusters, or the total SD), so give the one you want with sd:

apa_contrasts(fit_mixed, contrast = condition, sd = 12.5)

d is not computed for logistic regression and other generalized linear models, whose differences (e.g., in probabilities) are already on an interpretable scale.

Simple Slopes

A moderation analysis asks whether the effect of one predictor depends on another. In the mtcars data, the effect of a car’s weight on its fuel efficiency (miles per gallon) may depend on its horsepower:

d_mtcars <- mtcars |> 
  mutate(am = factor(am, 
                     levels = c(0,1), 
                     labels = c("Automatic", "Manual"))) |> 
  rename(MPG = mpg,
         Horsepower = hp,
         Weight = wt,
         Transmission = am)


fit_mod <- lm(MPG ~ Weight * Horsepower, data = d_mtcars)

apa_parameters(fit_mod) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Johnson–Neyman intervals (Johnson & Neyman, 1936): the slope of Weight is significant (p < .05) when Horsepower is from 52 to 236.48 (observed range: 52 to 335). CI = confidence interval.

Weight lowers fuel efficiency less in more powerful cars.

The notes of the simple-slopes tables above also give the Johnson–Neyman intervals: the values of horsepower, within its observed range, at which the slope of weight is significant. Rather than testing the slope at a few chosen values of the moderator, the Johnson–Neyman technique finds the values at which the slope’s test becomes significant, so readers can see where the effect holds. apa7 computes the boundaries exactly from the model’s coefficients and adds the intervals to the note whenever the slope depends on a single continuous moderator through a two-way interaction. Use johnson_neyman = FALSE to leave them out.

modelbased has shortcuts for common moderator values, and apa_slopes names the values they give. A numeric moderator named without values (by = "hp") is set to its mean and 1 standard deviation above and below it, as with by = "hp=[sd]":

apa_slopes(fit_mod, trend = Weight, by = Horsepower) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Other named shortcuts are "[quartiles]", "[minmax]", and "[mad]" (the median and 1 median absolute deviation above and below it). The shortcuts, and the default for a numeric variable named without values, work the same way in apa_means and apa_contrasts. For example, the difference between manual and automatic transmissions at three values of horsepower:

fit_am <- lm(MPG ~ Transmission * Horsepower, data = d_mtcars)

apa_contrasts(fit_am, contrast = Transmission, by = Horsepower) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Logistic Regression

For models with a link function, modelbased reports estimates on the response scale by default. For logistic regression, the estimates are probabilities, which have no leading zero in APA style, and the contrasts are differences in probabilities. The birthwt data set in the MASS package has the birth weights of 189 babies. Here, the probability of a low birth weight (under 2.5 kg) depends on the mother’s race, holding her weight at its mean and averaging over whether she smoked during pregnancy:

d_birth <- MASS::birthwt |> 
  mutate(race = factor(race, labels = c("White", "Black", "Other")),
         smoke = factor(smoke, labels = c("No", "Yes"))) |> 
  rename(low_birth_weight = low,
         mother_weight = lwt)

fit_logistic <- glm(
  low_birth_weight ~ race + smoke + mother_weight,
  data = d_birth,
  family = binomial
)

apa_means(fit_logistic, by = race) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Options

  • starred = "p" adds significance stars, and bolded = "p" bolds significant values, as in apa_parameters.
  • format_variable_names = FALSE keeps variable names exactly as they are.
  • effect_size = FALSE leaves Cohen’s d out of contrast tables, and sd sets the standard deviation it is computed with.
  • Bayesian models are not yet supported.
